title: the flute

segments.voice: Yesterday: Govardhan lifted. The storm came down on the village, and a boy held up a hill so everyone could shelter underneath.

A calf is drinking from its mother, and it stops. The milk is still in its mouth. It doesn't swallow. It just stands there, ears up. Somewhere past the pasture, among the trees, someone is playing a flute. That calf comes from the Bhagavata Purana, from a chapter where the women of Vraja, the gopis, stay behind in the village while Krishna takes the cows to the forest. They can't see him. They can only hear him. So they tell each other what the sound is doing to everything it reaches.
screen: `A CALF FORGETS TO SWALLOW.` → `A FLUTE IN THE TREES.` → `THE GOPIS CAN ONLY HEAR.`

segments.voice: In this chapter Krishna doesn't teach anyone. He just plays, walking into the autumn forest with his brother Balarama and the herd. The gopis fill in the picture from memory: a peacock feather in his hair, flowers at his ears, a yellow cloth, a garland of forest flowers, his lips on the bamboo. Then they turn to the listeners, and that list is the heart of the chapter. The cows lift their ears and drink in the sound; the calves stand with milk in their mouths. The birds settle on the branches and close their eyes. The does of the forest gaze at him, their mates beside them. The rivers, the gopis say, slow their current and reach out with their waves to hold his feet and offer him lotuses. Even the clouds, seeing him walk in the heat, drift over him to give him shade. Look at the audience. Not priests, not kings: cows, birds, deer, water, weather. Whatever hears the music stops what it was doing. And the gopis? At home, at their work, talking. The sound reaches them and he doesn't, so their delight and their ache come from the same place. Some devotional readers hear the whole world turned into a listener here, every creature called at once. Others hear a village falling in love with a sound. Either way, the chapter never explains the flute. It just shows what it does, down to a calf that forgets to swallow.

segments.voice: Let your eyes close or soften, and be one of the listeners in the forest: let sounds come to you, the room, the street, your own breath, without naming them. If a sound pulls you into thinking, come back with the next one. If you pray, let one sound stand for the flute, and listen to it as a call.
The flute. Krishna's bamboo flute, whose music, the gopis say, stops cows, birds, deer, rivers and clouds in the forest of Vraja.
Your line: the whole forest listening. Tomorrow, the gopis look at the flute itself. Day eight hundred ninety-seven, done.

howItsDone: Hindu art and temple images show Krishna holding a flute, and devotees sing songs about it at home and in temples; the Bhagavata's chapter on the flute is read aloud and sung in devotion.

chat.says: What's so special about Krishna's flute in that old story?
options: Its music stops cows, birds, rivers and clouds, and the gopis only hear it from home.
It's loud enough to call the whole herd home from miles across the hills.
It plays a secret tune that only the cowherd boys are able to hear.
